analysis.one_liner: Restores lower graduated estate tax rates and the unified credit for the very largest estates.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in August 1998, referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, and died there without a hearing or vote when Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal estate tax law already had low graduated rates and a credit that wipes out most tax on small and mid-sized estates, but a 1993 provision gradually took those benefits away from the very largest estates — a surcharge on wealth above roughly $17-24 million. This bill would repeal that phaseout, so the biggest estates would once again get the same low rates and credit everyone else does. It never moved past the committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Estates of people dying with taxable wealth high enough that the phaseout bites — roughly the top fraction of one percent of estates. The largest estates would save millions of dollars each in federal estate tax. Estate planning professionals would also gain a simpler, cheaper tax environment for their wealthiest clients.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Estates worth tens of millions of dollars

how_it_helps.text: The bill strikes the provision of tax law that phases out the 2-6% graduated estate tax rates and the unified credit for the largest estates, restoring those benefits for taxable estates above roughly $10-24 million depending on year [S2] [S3].
It applies retroactively to estates of people who died, and gifts made, after June 30, 1993, so it would reach estates already taxed over the prior five years, not just future deaths [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The U.S. Treasury — and by extension general taxpayers — would collect less estate tax revenue, since the phaseout is the mechanism that charges the very largest estates a higher effective rate. A retroactive effective date would claw back revenue from estates already settled.

drawbacks.text: The phaseout is the main surcharge on the very largest estates; repealing it cuts revenue precisely at the top, which is where the estate tax raises the most money per dollar of forgone base [S2] [S3].
The retroactive effective date (after June 30, 1993) means the change would not simply lower future taxes but would reopen settlements of estates already taxed, adding administrative complexity [S3].

A good-faith objection supporters would raise is that the phaseout creates a steep 'bubble' effective rate on very large estates and can complicate planning; an honest supporter would still have to concede the relief goes only to the largest estates, not to small family farms or businesses already sheltered by the credit.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but narrowly targeted: the only people who pay higher effective estate tax rates because of the phaseout are the largest estates, since smaller estates keep the graduated rates and unified credit regardless. The cost is federal revenue from the wealthiest estates, and the retroactive date would make the change more complicated to administer. As drafted, the relief flows almost entirely to the top of the wealth distribution.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in August 1998 and referred to the Ways and Means Committee, which never held a hearing or vote on it before the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Rep. Paul Gillmor introduced the bill on August 6, 1998, with Rep. Wally Herger as cosponsor [S3] [S4] [S5].
The House referred it to the Ways and Means Committee the same day; no further action is recorded [S5].
The Congress ended on January 3, 1999, and the bill died in committee without a vote [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The Treasury and general taxpayers kept the higher effective rates on the largest estates. The bill's intended beneficiaries — estates worth tens of millions — never got the tax cut.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The Treasury; large estates missed a tax cut

for.name: Rep. Paul Gillmor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the phaseout of the graduated estate tax rates and unified credit.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action — no hearing, markup, or vote — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Only two Republicans touched the bill (sponsor and one cosponsor) and it never reached a vote, so there is no record of how parties or the broader chamber would have split.

industries.note: The bill would restore the low graduated rates and unified credit for the largest estates, saving the biggest ones millions each. That gain comes directly out of federal tax revenue paid for by everyone else.

industries.industry: Estate planning and wealth advisory services
industries.note: A simpler rate structure for large estates reduces planning complexity for the industry's wealthiest clients and could expand demand for estate planning among families near the phaseout thresholds. The effect is modest compared with the direct tax saving to estates themselves.
Repealing the phaseout reduces estate tax revenue, which general taxpayers would make up through other taxes, future borrowing, or lower spending.
